title: LEMUR: Learned Multi-Vector Retrieval
claim: Multi-vector search can be reduced to fast single-vector search by pooling learned latent features, then reranking exactly.
layout: 2 rows, left-to-right; top block summary above detailed bottom flow
description: A two-tier horizontal pipeline diagram. The top row shows five colored rounded boxes joined by arrows: Query (blue), MLP (orange), ANNS index (pink), Top-k' candidate documents (green), and Top-k documents (purple). The bottom row expands each stage. On the left, a multi-vector representation X appears as a stack of blue token-row grids. A highlighted token embedding x feeds into a three-layer MLP drawn as columns of orange circles with dimensions R^d, R^d', R^m. A dashed arrow from the hidden layer points to the formula for the pooled single-vector representation Ψ(X), the sum of ψ(x). A curved arrow leads to a pink graph, the ANNS index. A k'-nn arrow leads to green document grids, and a MaxSim reranking arrow leads to the final document icons. Notation labels sit under each element.
caption: A schematic overview of the query-time process used by the LEMUR framework (for indexing, see Section 3). The latent representations ψ(x) of the token-level embeddings x ∈X are obtained from the hidden layer of an MLP trained to estimate the MaxSim similarities between a query and each document. The single-vector representation Ψ(X) is obtained by pooling these latent representations. The k′ documents most similar to Ψ(X) are retrieved using an ANNS index. The final top-k documents are selected by evaluating the exact MaxSim similarities to these k′ documents.
abstract: Multi-vector representations generated by late interaction models, such as ColBERT, enable superior retrieval quality compared to single-vector representations in information retrieval applications. In multi-vector retrieval systems, both queries and documents are encoded using one embedding per token, and similarity between queries and documents is measured by the MaxSim similarity measure. However, the improved quality of multi-vector retrieval comes at the expense of significantly increased search latency. In this work, we introduce LEMUR, a simple yet efficient framework for multi-vector similarity search. LEMUR consists of two consecutive problem reductions: First, we formulate multi-vector similarity search as a supervised learning problem that can be solved using a one-hidden-layer neural network. Second, we reduce inference under this model to single-vector similarity search in its latent space, enabling the use of existing single-vector search indexes to accelerate retrieval. LEMUR is an order of magnitude faster than prior multi-vector similarity search methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ejaasaari/lemur
